questions.question: What does overriding `ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)` in a `BackgroundService` give you?
options: A method that runs once per HTTP request
A place for work that runs for the entire lifetime of the app, independent of any individual request
A way to handle exceptions globally
A method that only runs in development
questions.explanation: ExecuteAsync starts when the app starts and (typically via a loop) continues running until the app shuts down — it has nothing to do with individual HTTP requests.

questions.question: Why should a BackgroundService's loop check `stoppingToken` and pass it into `await` calls?
options: It's optional decoration with no real effect
So the worker stops promptly when the app is shutting down, instead of blocking shutdown or continuing to run after the app should have stopped
It makes the loop run faster
It's required syntax that does nothing functionally
questions.explanation: stoppingToken is signaled during app shutdown. Checking it (and passing it to Task.Delay/PeriodicTimer waits) lets the background work exit promptly rather than delaying shutdown or running past when it should stop.

questions.question: A BackgroundService is a singleton, but it needs to use a Scoped DbContext. What's the correct approach?
options: Inject the DbContext directly into the BackgroundService's constructor
Inject IServiceProvider, then call CreateScope() each time you need the scoped service, disposing the scope afterward
Change the DbContext's lifetime to Singleton
It's impossible to use a DbContext inside a BackgroundService
questions.explanation: A long-lived singleton can't safely hold a long-lived reference to a Scoped service. Creating a fresh scope per unit of work (each loop iteration, for instance) is the standard, safe pattern.

questions.question: What does `Channel<T>` provide that a plain `List<T>` doesn't, for a producer/consumer scenario?
options: Nothing, they're interchangeable
Thread-safe, async-friendly writing and reading — multiple producers can safely write concurrently, and a consumer can `await foreach` items as they arrive
Channel<T> is just a faster List<T>
Channel<T> only works with strings
questions.explanation: A List<T> isn't safe for concurrent access and has no built-in way to asynchronously wait for new items to appear. Channel<T> is purpose-built for exactly this: safe concurrent writes and an async stream of reads.

questions.question: Why might an API endpoint write to a Channel<T> instead of doing slow work (like sending an email) directly?
options: It's required syntax for all endpoints
It lets the endpoint respond immediately after queuing the work, while a separate background worker actually performs the slow operation at its own pace
Channels make the email send faster
There's no benefit
questions.explanation: This decouples 'the request is queued' from 'the work is done' — the caller gets a fast response, and the actual (possibly slow) work happens asynchronously in the background, processed by a BackgroundService reading from the channel.

questions.question: `PeriodicTimer` combined with `WaitForNextTickAsync` is a purpose-built alternative to manually looping with `Task.Delay` for recurring, scheduled work.
questions.explanation: PeriodicTimer is specifically designed for 'run this every N seconds/minutes' scenarios, and WaitForNextTickAsync cleanly returns false on cancellation, ending the loop without extra manual checks.
